Among them also: it is established in the Sahih that "on the day of the conquest of Makkah, he (ﷺ) placed Khalid ibn al-Walid over the right wing, placed al-Zubayr over the left wing, and placed Abu 'Ubaydah over the infantry (*al-hussar*). They took the bottom of the valley. Then he said: 'O Abu Hurayrah, call the Ansar for me.' They came running, and he said: 'O company of the Ansar, do you see the rabble of Quraysh?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Look, when you meet them tomorrow, mow them down with a mowing.' He hid it with his hand and placed his right hand on his left, and said: 'Your meeting place is al-Safa.' The Ansar came and surrounded al-Safa. He said: 'No one who raised his head that day was spared except that they put him to sleep.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa, and the Ansar came and surrounded al-Safa. Then Abu Sufyan came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the green of Quraysh has been destroyed, there is no Quraysh after today.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, whoever lays down his weapons is safe, and whoever closes his door is safe.'"

Muslim recorded it in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

The historians of the campaigns (*ahl al-maghazi*) detailed what was summarized in this hadith of Muslim. They clarified that twelve of the disbelievers were killed, and it was said that twenty-four of Quraysh and four of Hudhayl were killed. Three of the Muslims were killed that day: Salamah ibn al-Mayla' al-Juhani, Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi, attributed to Muharib ibn Fihr, and Khunays ibn Khalid al-Khuza'i, brother of Umm Ma'bad. Kurz said before he was killed while defending Khunays:

*"The fair-skinned one of the Banu Fihr has known,*
*Pure of complexion and pure of heart,*
*That I will surely strike today on behalf of Abu Sakhr."*

In it is the transfer of the vowel in pausal position (*naql al-haraka fi al-waqf*). The well-known verse of Hamas ibn Qays indicates fighting on the day of the conquest, and al-Shinqiti mentioned it in his *Maghazi* with the words:

*"Ibn Qays claimed that he would make their women his slaves, so I said to him, and I recited:*
*If they come forward today, I have no excuse. This is a complete weapon, and an instrument of war.*
*And one with two blades, quick in drawing.*
*He witnessed the narrow pass in which Hutama was present,*
*A man of his people who fled in defeat.*
*And the Virgin came and locked her door, so she asked him, whatever you were saying..."*

[The rest of the verse, as the text continues in the source, is quoted in the same rhythm and is translated above in its sense: the speaker recalls the flight of Safwan and 'Ikrimah at the Day of al-Khandamah, and the Muslims' swords striking heads and skulls, and tells the woman not to utter any word of blame.]

This verse is explicit that fighting and killing occurred on the day of the conquest of Makkah, and its confirmation is in the Sahih as already mentioned.

Among them also: Umm Hani', daughter of Abu Talib (may Allah be pleased with her), granted protection to a man, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) wanted to kill him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have granted protection to whomever you have protected, O Umm Hani'." In another wording from her: "When the day of the conquest of Makkah came, I granted protection to two men from my in-laws, and I put them in a house and locked a door upon them. Then my maternal brother 'Ali came at me, and I stood over them with the sword..." She mentioned the hadith of the safe-conduct and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have granted protection to whomever you have protected, O Umm Hani'." That was in the forenoon, in the lowland of Makkah after the conquest, and her story is established in the Sahih.

Her granting of protection, 'Ali's (may Allah be pleased with him) intention to kill him, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) confirmation of her protection, are explicit that it was taken by force.

Among them: he (ﷺ) ordered the killing of Miqyas ibn Subabah, Ibn Khatal, and two singing girls.

Had it been taken by treaty, none of its people would have been ordered killed, and the mention of these would have been an exception to the terms of the treaty.

His (ﷺ) order to kill those mentioned is established from him (ﷺ). \ 5 And in the Sunan with a sound chain: "When the day of the conquest of Makkah came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Grant safety to the people, except two women and four men; kill them even if you find them clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah.'" And other proofs besides these.

These are clear proofs that Makkah, may Allah protect it, was taken by force.

That Makkah was taken by force undermines the position of al-Shafi'i that it is obligatory to divide conquered land taken by force.

What all the evidences agree upon, with no contradiction among them, is what we have already stated regarding the option between dividing the land and leaving it for the Muslims, together with the arguments we have already presented. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Having understood that the verified position is that Makkah was taken by force, know that the scholars differed concerning the houses (*ribā'*, sing. *rib'*, dwellings and plots) of Makkah: is it permissible to own them, sell them, and rent them out? There are three views:

The first: none of this is permissible. This was the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Mujahid, 'Ata', Tawus, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, Ishaq, and others.

Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) disliked it.

Al-Shafi'i and Abu Yusuf permitted all of this.

This was also the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and a group of the Companions and those after them.

Imam Ahmad took a middle course, saying: they may be owned and inherited, but not rented out or sold, according to one of the two narrations, reconciling the evidences. The second narration is the same as the position of al-Shafi'i.

* *

This question was debated by Imam al-Shafi'i and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh in the Mosque of al-Khayf, while Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal was present. Al-Shafi'i silenced Ishaq with evidences, after he said to him: "How much I wish that someone other than you were in your position, for I would order that his ears be twisted. I say to you: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and you say: Tawus said, al-Hasan said, Ibrahim said. Does anyone have a proof alongside the Prophet (ﷺ)?" in a lengthy discussion.

We will mention, if Allah wills, the evidences of all of them, and which of them the evidence indicates to be preferred.

(p-74) The argument of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) and those who agree with him rests on several points:

The first: the hadith of Usamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), when he asked him: "Where will you stay tomorrow?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Has 'Aqil left us any houses or dwellings?" In some narrations it is "any dwelling," and in some "a dwelling." Al-Bukhari recorded this hadith in the Book of Hajj, in the chapter "The Inheritance of the Houses of Makkah and Their Purchase," etc.; and in the Book of Campaigns, in the section on the conquest campaign in Ramadan, in the chapter "Where the Prophet (ﷺ) planted the banner on the day of the conquest"; and in the Book of Jihad, in the chapter "If a people embrace Islam in the land of war, and they have property and lands, then these are theirs." Muslim recorded it in the Book of Hajj, in the chapter "Lodging in Makkah for the Pilgrim and the Inheritance of its Houses," with three narrations similar to those of al-Bukhari.

So his (ﷺ) saying in this agreed-upon hadith: "Has 'Aqil left us any dwellings?" is explicit that he (ﷺ) approved the sale by 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) of those dwellings.

Had their sale and ownership not been valid, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have approved it, because he does not approve of falsehood, by the consensus of the Muslims.

The second reason: Allah, blessed and exalted, attributed to the emigrants from Makkah their homes (diyar), and this indicates that these were their property, in His saying: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ [al-Hashr: 8].

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* (*Explanation of al-Muhadhdhab*): If it is said that the attribution may refer to possession (yad) and residence, as in His saying: ﴿And abide in your houses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33].

The answer is that the true meaning of attribution (idafah) requires ownership. For this reason, if someone says, "This house belongs to Zayd," it is ruled that its ownership belongs to Zayd. If he then says, "I meant by it residence and possession only," it is not accepted.

A parallel to the noble verse is what was also cited as evidence from the attribution in his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe," the hadith. We have previously mentioned that it is in *Sahih Muslim*.

The third reason: the well-known report in the *Sunan* of al-Bayhaqi and others: "Nafi' ibn al-Harith bought the prison house for Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) from Safwan ibn Umayyah for four hundred," and in another narration, "for four thousand." No one among the Companions denied this.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar and al-Bayhaqi also narrated that Hakim ibn Hizam (may Allah be pleased with him) sold Dar al-Nadwah in Makkah to Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan for one hundred thousand. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said to him: "O Abu Khalid, you have sold the glory (ma'thara) and the nobility of Quraysh!" He replied: "Far off! The noble deeds have gone; there is no noble deed today except Islam." Then he said: "Bear witness that it is in the way of Allah, the Exalted," meaning the dirhams for which he sold it.

Shaykh Ahmad al-Badawi al-Shinqiti set this in his versified *Amud al-Nasab* (*The Pillar of Lineage*) with the words, meaning Qusayy:

*He took the Nadwah, and nothing is invented*
*in other than it, nor is any matter decided,*
*the girl or the boy is not excused*
*except by his command, for it is sought.*
*Then Hakim ibn Hizam sold it,*
*and they rebuked him, and the lord (al-Hammam) gave it all in charity,*
*the chief of his assembly, with the whole price,*
*for glory is by religion, not by ruins.*

The fourth reason: that it was conquered by capitulation (sulh), so it remained in the ownership of its people. We have previously mentioned the weakness of this view.

The fifth reason: analogy (qiyas), because the land of Makkah is living land (ard hayyah) and not endowed (mawqufah), so it is permissible to sell it by analogy with other lands.

Those who held that the houses of Makkah cannot be owned or sold argued with evidences:

Among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Sacred Mosque which We have made for the people, equal therein are the resident and the visitor﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. They said: the intended meaning of "the Mosque" is the entire Haram, because it is frequently used for it in the texts, such as:

- His saying: ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra: 1], the verse;
- His saying: ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7], the verse;
- His saying: ﴿As an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95].

Yet the principal place of sacrifice in the Haram is Mina.

Among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾ [al-Naml: 91]. They said: what is made sacred may not be sold.

Among them is what al-Bayhaqi narrated through the chain of Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhajir, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Babah, from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Makkah is a resting-place (munakh); its houses may not be sold, nor their rent taken."

Among them is what Abu Hanifah narrated from Ubaydullah ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Najih, from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Makkah is sacred, and the sale of its houses is forbidden, and the hire of its houses is forbidden."

(p-76) Among them is what was reported from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we not build you a house, or a structure that shades you from the sun?' He said: 'No, it is only a resting-place for whoever arrives first.'" Abu Dawud narrated it.

Among them is what al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Majah narrated from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Alqamah ibn Nadlah al-Kinani, who said: "The houses of Makkah were called al-sawa'ib (the free ones). Their houses were not sold in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor of Abu Bakr, nor of Umar. Whoever was in need dwelt, and whoever was well-off let others dwell."

Among them is what was reported from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her): that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mina is a resting-place for whoever arrives first."

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, in the Book of Funerals, in the chapter on burial, concerning this hadith: It was narrated by Abu Muhammad al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and others, through sound chains from the narration of Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her).

Al-Tirmidhi said: It is a hasan hadith.

He mentioned in the Book of Sales, in the discussion of selling the houses of Makkah and other lands of the Haram, that this hadith is sahih.

Among them is what Abd al-Razzaq ibn Mujahid narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "Ata used to forbid renting in the Haram, and he informed me that Umar ibn al-Khattab used to forbid the fitting of doors to the houses of Makkah, so that the pilgrims could stay in their open spaces. The first to fit a door to his house was Suhayl ibn Amr, so Umar ibn al-Khattab sent to him about that. He said: 'Give me a respite, O Commander of the Believers, for I was a merchant, and I wished to make two doors to shield my back.' He said: 'Then that is for you.'"

Abd al-Razzaq also said, from Ma'mar, from Mansur, from Mujahid, that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O people of Makkah, do not make doors for your houses, so that the desert-dweller may alight wherever he wishes." End of quotation. Ibn Kathir said this, and there are other evidences besides these.

The writer of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The strongest of the views in evidence, as appears, is the saying of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him, because of the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd, agreed upon, as we have mentioned, and because of the other evidences we have mentioned. Also, all the people of Makkah retained their homes after the conquest, doing with them what they wished, by sale, rent, and other means.

Those who held this sound view answered the evidences of the opposing side. As for His saying: (p-77) ﴿equal therein are the resident and the visitor﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], they answered that the intended meaning is specifically the Mosque to the exclusion of the rest of the land of the Haram, as evidenced by the explicit mention of the Mosque itself in His saying: ﴿And the Sacred Mosque which We have made for the people, equal﴾, the verse [al-Hajj: 25]. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿this city, who has made it sacred﴾ [al-Naml: 91], they answered that the intended meaning is: He made sacred its game, its trees, its grass, and fighting within it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) explained in the sound hadiths. In none of them, despite their number, is there a prohibition on selling its houses.

As for the hadith of Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhajir from his father, it is weak. Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: It is weak by the agreement of the hadith scholars, and they agreed on the weakness of Isma'il and his father Ibrahim. End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*: Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhajir is weak, and his father is not strong. It was reported from him in different ways: it was reported from him thus, and it was reported from him from his father, from Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr, raised (marfu') in part of its meaning. As for the hadith of Aishah, it is to be understood as referring to the dead land (mawat) of the Haram.

Al-Nawawi said: This is the apparent meaning of the hadith.

As for the hadith of Abu Hanifah: it is weak on two counts:

The first: the weakness of its chain because of Ibn Abi Ziyad mentioned in it.

The second: that the correct version according to the memorizers is that it is mawquf (stopping at Companion level) on Abdullah ibn Umar. They said: its being raised is an error. This was said by al-Daraqutni, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and al-Bayhaqi.

As for the hadith of Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, there are two answers:

The first: that it is munqati' (disconnected), as al-Bayhaqi said.

The second: what al-Bayhaqi also said, and a group of the Shafi'is and others: that the intended meaning of the hadith is to report their noble custom of lodging, by lending freely out of generosity, what they did not need of their houses.

Yet one who knew more than him about the state of Makkah reported the operation of inheritance and sale in it.

As for the hadith "Mina is a resting-place for whoever arrives first," it is to be understood as referring to its dead land and the places where pilgrims alight, as al-Nawawi said. End of quotation.

Know that al-Bayhaqi's weakening of the hadith of Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhajir, and the hadith of (p-78) Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman from Alqamah ibn Nadlah, was critiqued by its annotator, the author of *al-Jawhar al-Naqi*, with this text: "He mentioned in it a hadith whose chain contains Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhajir. He weakened Isma'il, and said that from his father he was not strong. Then he cited it from another route, then said: its being raised is an error, and the correct version is mawquf. I say: al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* narrated this hadith from the two routes that al-Bayhaqi mentioned, then he authenticated the first and took the second as a corroboration of it. Then al-Bayhaqi mentioned at its end a hadith from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman from Alqamah ibn Nadlah, then said: this is munqati'. I say: this hadith was narrated by Ibn Majah with a chain meeting the conditions of Muslim, and al-Daraqutni and others narrated it. This Alqamah is a Companion, as the scholars of this discipline mention. When a Companion says words like this, it is raised (marfu') according to what is known of it. And in it Uthman explicitly states hearing from Alqamah, so where is the disconnection?" End of the words of the author of *al-Jawhar al-Naqi*.

The writer of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The objection of Ibn al-Turkmani against al-Hafiz al-Bayhaqi in his weakening of the two hadiths mentioned is clearly untenable.

As for the first: al-Hakim's authentication, may Allah have mercy on him, of a weak hadith does not make it sound.

How many weak hadiths did al-Hakim, may Allah have mercy on him, authenticate! His leniency in authentication is well known among the scholars of hadith. As for Ibrahim ibn Muhajir ibn Jabir al-Bajali, there may be some ground for debate over weakening a hadith by him, because some scholars of the men (of hadith) declared him trustworthy, and he is among the narrators of Muslim.

But Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, with weak memory." As for his son Isma'il, there is no disagreement that he is weak, and weakening the hadith by him is evident and beyond challenge.

Ibn Hajar also said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Weak." Therefore, authenticating this hadith has no basis.

As for his statement in his objection about al-Bayhaqi's weakening of the second hadith, "where is the disconnection?" — its answer is that the disconnection lies in that Alqamah ibn Nadlah is a minor Successor (tabi'i saghir). The claim of Shaykh Ibn al-Turkmani that he is a Companion is not correct. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Alqamah ibn Nadlah — with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the marked letter — the Makki, Kinani." It was also said: "Kindi, a minor Successor, acceptable. Whoever counted him among the Companions was mistaken." In that case, the route of his disconnection is evident. Thus it is clear that the correct view is with al-Hafiz al-Bayhaqi, al-Nawawi, and others in weakening (p-79) the two hadiths mentioned.

There is no doubt that whoever abstains from selling or renting the houses of Makkah, to leave the disagreement, that is better for him, because whoever avoids doubtful matters has cleared his religion and his honour.

Note (tanbih)

All Muslims agree that the places of the rites (nusuk) in the Haram, such as the place of sa'y (running between Safa and Marwah) and the place of throwing the pebbles (rami al-jimar), have the ruling of mosques, and all Muslims are equal in them.

It is apparent that what the pilgrims need of Mina and Muzdalifah is likewise. It is not permissible for anyone to narrow them by building on private property until they become too cramped for the pilgrims, and some of them find no lodging, because spending the night at Muzdalifah on the night of sacrifice, and at Mina on the nights of the Days of Tashriq, are among the rites of Hajj.

So it is not permissible for anyone to restrict the place of the rites from the Muslims, to the point that no room remains that can hold all the pilgrims. The hadith "Mina is a resting-place for whoever arrives first" supports this, as already mentioned.

The fifth issue: an investigation of what the Imam may grant to a person from the spoils (ghanimah). We will mention the views of the scholars on this and their evidences, and what the evidence indicates as more preponderant.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 8, verse 41 (part 6 of 7):

Know that the scholars differed on this question, as we indicated at the beginning of this noble surah, and we promised to clarify it here. Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the imam may not grant anyone a special reward (tanfil, an extra share from the spoils) except from the khums (one-fifth). This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, because the remaining four-fifths belong to the warriors who obtained them by advancing upon them with horses and mounts. This is the well-known position of his school. He also had another view: that the tanfil may be taken from the khums of the khums.

The basis of this view is that the four parts of the khums, apart from the Messenger's khums (ﷺ), are for specified recipients, as in His words: ﴿and for the kinsfolk, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer﴾, while the remaining four-fifths belong to the warriors.

The most sound of the views reported from al-Shafi'i is that the imam grants tanfil only from the khums of the khums. His evidence is what we mentioned just above.

It is reported from Amr ibn Shu'ayb that he said: "There is no tanfil after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Ibn Qudama said in al-Mughni: "Perhaps he relies on His words, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾." (p-٨٠)

Imam Ahmad, together with a group of scholars, held that the imam may grant a quarter after the khums at the beginning of the campaign (al-badʾah), and a third after the khums on the return (al-rajʿah).

The position of Abu Hanifa is that before the spoils are secured, the imam may grant a quarter, a third, more or less after the khums. After the spoils have been secured, he may not grant tanfil except from the khums.

We have already set out the general course of the disagreement on this question at the beginning of this noble surah. We now mention, God willing, what the evidence indicates to be the stronger view.

Know first that the tanfil whose permissibility the evidence indicates takes several forms.

The first: the imam says to a group of the army, "If you take any booty from the unbelievers, you will have such-and-such from it after its khums is removed." This is permissible. He may grant them a quarter when the Muslim army is advancing against the unbelievers, and a third when the Muslim army is returning to its homelands, after the khums is removed.

Malik and his companions say that this is not permissible, because it causes the corruption of the intentions of the fighters, since they become fighters for the sake of the wealth which the imam has promised them as tanfil.

The evidence for its permissibility is what Habib ibn Maslama ibn Malik al-Qurashi al-Fihri narrated: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) granted a quarter after the khums at the beginning of the campaign, and granted a third after the khums on the return." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah, and authenticated by Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and Ibn al-Jarud.

Know that the verified view concerning the aforementioned Habib is that he was a companion (sahabi). Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: "His companionship is disputed, and the stronger view is that it is established, but he was young, and he is mentioned in the Sahih in the hadith of Ibn Umar with Mu'awiya." End of quotation.

Abu Dawud narrated this hadith from him through three chains. Among them: from Makhul ibn Abd Allah al-Shami, who said: "I was a slave in Egypt to a woman from the Banu Hudhayl, and she freed me. I did not leave Egypt without having gathered whatever knowledge was there, as I believed. Then I came to the Hijaz, and I did not leave it without having gathered whatever knowledge was there, as I believed. Then I came to Iraq, and I did not leave it without having gathered whatever knowledge was there, as I believed. Then I came to Syria and sifted it thoroughly. In all of this I was asking about tanfil, but I did not find anyone who informed me of anything concerning it, until I met a shaykh called Ziyad ibn (p-٨١) Jariya al-Tamimi. I said to him: 'Have you heard anything about tanfil?' He said: 'Yes, I heard Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri say: I witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) grant a quarter at the beginning of the campaign and a third on the return.'" End of quotation.

We have already established that the sound view is that he was a companion, and in this narration he explicitly states that he witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) granting a quarter, to the end of the hadith.

Among the evidence for this also is what Ubada ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) used to grant a quarter at the beginning of the campaign and a third on the return." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and authenticated by Ibn Hibban.

In a narration in Imam Ahmad's collection: "When he set out into enemy territory, he granted a quarter; and when he turned back and all the people were returning, he granted a third. He disliked tanfil and used to say: 'Let the strong among the believers return to the weak among them.'"

These texts indicate that tanfil from outside the khums is established.

Also supporting this is what Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated from Ma'n ibn Yazid, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'There is no tanfil except after the khums.'" Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: "al-Tahawi authenticated this hadith." End of quotation.

The difference between the beginning of the campaign and the return is this: at the beginning, the Muslims are heading into the lands of the enemy, and the enemy is heedless. On the return, the Muslims are returning to their homelands from enemy territory, and the enemy is on guard and alert. There is a clear difference between the two situations.

The aforementioned hadiths indicate that when a detachment (sariyya) from the army sets out and obtains booty, the rest of the army are its partners. There is no disagreement among the scholars on this, as al-Qurtubi said.

The second of the forms of tanfil whose permissibility the evidence indicates is granting a special share to some of the army because of their exceptional valour, their hardship, and their bearing of what others did not bear. The evidence for this is what is established in Sahih Muslim, and was narrated by Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud, from Salama ibn al-Akwa', may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the raid of Abd al-Rahman al-Fazari upon the herd of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his recovery of it from him. Salama said: "When morning came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The best of our horsemen today is Abu Qatada, and the best of our foot soldiers is Salama.'" He said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me two shares: the share of the horseman and the share of the foot soldier, and he combined them for me (p-٨٢) entirely." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih, from a long hadith.

We have already mentioned that this was the raid of Dhi Qarad, in the Surah of al-Nisa'. Also supporting this is the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah, in which Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Perhaps he will give this sword to a man who did not show my valour." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it to Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, because of his good conduct and his killing of the owner of the sword, as was mentioned earlier.

The third of the forms of tanfil whose permissibility the evidence indicates is that the imam says: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, his spoils (salab) belong to him."

Among the evidence for this is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their Sahihs from Abu Qatada, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Hunayn. When we met the enemy, the Muslims suffered a setback. I saw a man from the polytheists overpowering a man from the Muslims, so I circled around to him until I reached him from behind, and struck him on the joint of his shoulder. He turned on me and embraced me in an embrace whose smell I found to be the smell of death. Then death overtook him, and he released me. I caught up with Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he said: 'What is wrong with the people?' I said: 'The command of Allah.' Then the people returned, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat down and said: 'Whoever kills a slain enemy for whom he has proof, his spoils belong to him.' So I stood up, then said: 'Who will testify for me?' Then I sat down. Then he said the same thing, and I stood up and said: 'Who will testify for me?' Then I sat down. Then he said that a third time, and I stood up. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What is the matter with you, Abu Qatada?' I related the story to him. A man from the people said: 'He has spoken the truth, O Messenger of Allah, and the spoils of that slain man are with me; so satisfy him from his right.' Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'No, by Allah, he would not deliberately go to a lion from the lions of Allah who fights for Allah and His Messenger, and then have him give you his spoils.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'He has spoken the truth; give them to him.' So he gave them to me. I sold the armour and bought with its price an orchard in the Banu Salima. This was indeed the first wealth I acquired in Islam." There are many hadiths to this effect.

Abu Dawud and Ahmad narrated from Anas that on the day of Hunayn Abu Talha killed twenty men and took their spoils. In another narration from him in Ahmad's collection, it says twenty-one. The historians of the military campaigns mention that Abu Talha said, regarding those he killed, [Rajaz meter]:

"I am Abu Talha, and my name is Zayd,
And every day there is game in my weapons."

The truth is that it is not a condition in this that it be in a single combat, nor that the slain unbeliever be advancing (p-٨٣) toward him.

As for the evidence that single combat is not a condition, it is this hadith of Abu Qatada, which is agreed upon.

As for the evidence that it is not a condition that he killed him while the man was advancing toward him, it is the hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwa', who said: "We fought with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against Hawazin. While we were having our midday meal with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a man came riding a red camel. He made it kneel, then pulled a rope from his waist and tied the camel with it. Then he went forward to eat with the people, looking around, and among us were weak people and those with weak backs, and some of us were on foot. Then he suddenly came out running, reached his camel, untied its rope, made it kneel, sat on it, and stirred it, so the camel rushed off with him. A man followed him on a speckled she-camel. Salama said: 'I went out running, and I was beside the flank of the she-camel. Then I advanced until I was beside the flank of the camel. Then I advanced until I took hold of the camel's halter and made it kneel. When it placed its knee on the ground, I drew my sword and struck the man's head with it, and it fell. Then I came with the camel leading it, and on it was its saddle and its weapons. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me, with the people behind him, and said: "Who killed the man?" They said: "Ibn al-Akwa'." He said: "His spoils belong entirely to him."'" Agreed upon. The wording mentioned is that of Muslim in the Book of Jihad and Military Expeditions, under the chapter "The Killer's Entitlement to the Spoils of the Slain." Al-Bukhari narrated it in meaning in the Book of Jihad, under the chapter "The Harbi (enemy combatant) who enters the abode of Islam without a safe-conduct." It is explicit that single combat is not a condition, nor is it a condition that he be killed while advancing rather than retreating, as you see.

The killer does not deserve the spoils of the slain unless the slain was one of the combatants whom it is permissible to fight.

As for one who kills a woman, a child, a decrepit old man, or a feeble and contemptible person, or one who has been severely wounded with no benefit left in him, he has no right to his spoils.

There is no disagreement among the scholars that whoever kills a child, a woman, or a decrepit old man does not deserve their spoils, except for a very weak view reported from Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir concerning the entitlement to the spoils of a woman.

The evidence that whoever kills one who has been severely wounded does not deserve his spoils is that Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was the one who finished off Abu Jahl on the day of Badr and cut off his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) had already awarded his spoils to Mu'adh ibn Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who had inflicted the wound, and he gave Ibn Mas'ud nothing.

This is the truth brought by the agreed-upon hadith, so it is not to be opposed by what Imam Ahmad (p-٨٤) and Abu Dawud narrated "from Ibn Mas'ud: 'That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted him the sword of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr'," because it comes from the narration of his son Abu Ubayda, who did not hear it from him. Likewise, one who is brought forward for execution in cold blood does not entitle his killer to his spoils, because the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the execution in cold blood of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith al-Abdari and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt al-Umawi on the day of Badr, and he did not give those who killed them any of their spoils.

The scholars differed about one who takes a captive: is he entitled to the captive's spoils, by analogy between capture and killing, or not? The apparent view is that he is not entitled to them, for lack of evidence. Therefore it is obligatory to hold to the generality of His words: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils﴾, and the rest of the verse, until a specifying text comes from the Book or a sound Sunna. The Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims took captives at Badr, and some of them were executed in cold blood, as we have mentioned. He did not give any of those who captured them any of their spoils or of their ransom; rather, he made their ransom part of the booty.

If the woman or the child fights the Muslims, the apparent ruling is that whoever kills one of them takes his spoils (salab), because at that point he is someone whose killing is permitted. So he falls under the general wording of "whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils," the hadith. Other scholars have also firmly held this view, and God knows best.

Know that the scholars differed over whether the killer's entitlement to the spoils (salab) depends on the leader's statement, "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils," or whether he is entitled to them unconditionally, whether or not the leader said it.

Among those who held the latter view are Imam Ahmad, al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Thawr, al-Tabari, and Ibn al-Mundhir.

Among those who held the former view, that he is not entitled to it except by the leader's saying, "Whoever kills an enemy..." etc., are Imam Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Thawri.

We have already mentioned from Malik and his companions that the leader's saying this is not permitted before the fighting, lest it lead to corruption of intention. But after the event has occurred, the leader says, "Whoever kills an enemy..." etc.

Those who held that the killer is entitled to the victim's spoils unconditionally argued from the generality of the evidence, since the Prophet (ﷺ) stated explicitly that whoever kills an enemy has his spoils, and this was not restricted by anything. The determining factor is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion, as is known in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

Malik, Abu Hanifa, and those who agreed with them argued with several pieces of evidence:

Among them is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', the agreed-upon hadith mentioned earlier: "He has his spoils entirely." They said: if the spoils were due to him simply by killing, he would not have needed to repeat this statement.

Among them is the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, agreed upon, concerning the killing of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr by Mu'adh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu'adh ibn 'Afra', the two Ansari men. In it: "Then the two of them turned back to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: 'Which of you killed him?' Each of them said: 'I killed him.' He said: 'Have you wiped your swords?' They said: 'No.' He looked at the two swords and said: 'Both of you killed him,' and he awarded his spoils to Mu'adh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh." End of quote.

They said: the Prophet's (ﷺ) explicit statement in this agreed-upon hadith, that both of them killed him, and then his specifying the spoils for one of them and not the other, is clear that the killer is not entitled to the spoils except by the leader's saying that they are his. For if his entitlement were due merely to the killing, there would be no reason to deny Mu'adh ibn 'Afra', since the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly said that he killed him together with Mu'adh ibn 'Amr, and he would have divided it between them.

Among them is what Imam Ahmad, Muslim, and Abu Dawud narrated from Awf ibn Malik, who said: "A man from Himyar killed a man from the enemy, and he wanted his spoils, but Khalid ibn al-Walid, who was governor over them, prevented him. Awf ibn Malik went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him. He said to Khalid: 'What prevented you from giving him his spoils?' He said: 'I considered it too much, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'Give it to him.' Khalid passed by Awf and pulled his cloak, then said: 'Have you accomplished what I mentioned to you from the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?' Awf became angry and said: 'Do not give it to him, O Khalid, do not give it to him, O Khalid! Will you leave my commanders to me? Your likeness and theirs is like a man who was entrusted with camels or sheep and tended them, then he awaited the time for watering them, brought them to a basin, and they drank its clear water and left its turbid water. Its clear water is for you, and its turbid water is for them.'"

In another narration with Muslim also, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "I went out with those who went out with Zayd ibn Harithah on the expedition of Mu'tah, and a reinforcement from Yemen accompanied me." He related the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) in similar form, except that he said in the hadith: Awf ibn Malik said: "I said: 'O Khalid, do you not know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) decided that the spoils belong to the killer?' He said: 'Yes, but I considered it too much.'" This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih.

In another narration from Awf, also in the works of Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud, he said: "I went out with Zayd ibn Harithah on the expedition of Mu'tah, and a reinforcement from the people of Yemen accompanied me." We proceeded and met the Byzantine (Rum) armies, and among them was a man on a chestnut horse, with a gilded saddle and gilded weapons. The Byzantine kept slaughtering among the Muslims. The reinforcement from Yemen lay in wait for him behind a rock. The Byzantine passed by him, and he hamstrung his horse, so it fell, and he overpowered him and killed him. He seized his horse and weapons. When God, Mighty and Majestic, granted victory to the Muslims, Khalid ibn al-Walid sent for him and took the spoils. Awf said: "I came to him and said: 'O Khalid, do you not know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) decided that the spoils belong to the killer?' He said: 'Yes, but I considered it too much.' I said: 'You must return it to him, or I will report you to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).' He refused to return it to him." Awf said: "We gathered before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I related to him the story of the Yemeni reinforcement and what Khalid did." He mentioned the rest of the hadith with a meaning similar to what preceded. End of quote.

So the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in this sound hadith, "Do not give it to him, O Khalid," is evidence that he did not become entitled to the spoils merely by killing. For if he had been entitled to it by that, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have prevented him from it.

Among them is what Ibn Abi Shaybah related, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Bishr ibn 'Alqamah, who said: "I fought a man on the day of al-Qadisiyyah, killed him, and took his spoils. I came to Sa'd, and Sa'd addressed his companions, then said: 'This is the spoils of Bishr ibn 'Alqamah, and it is worth more than twelve thousand dirhams, and we have given it to him as a reward.'"

So if the spoils belonged to the killer by a judgment from the Prophet (ﷺ), the commanders would not have attributed that grant to their own opinion and independent judgment, and the killer would have taken it without their order. This was stated by al-Qurtubi.

The author of this commentary, may God pardon him, says: the stronger of the two opinions in my view, in terms of evidence, is that the killer is not entitled to the spoils except by the leader's giving them, on account of these sound pieces of evidence that we have mentioned. If it is said: these support the view of Ishaq, that if the spoils are small they belong to the killer, and if they are large one-fifth is taken from them.

The answer: its apparent meaning is general, and moreover the spoils of Abu Jahl did not contain any additional large amount, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prevented Mu'adh ibn 'Afra' from it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 8, verse 45:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you encounter a company (fi'ah), then stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may succeed.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted commands the believers to stand firm when they meet the enemy and to remember Allah much, indicating that this is a cause of success (falah). The command to do something is a prohibition of its opposite, or it necessarily implies a prohibition of its opposite, as is known in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Thus the noble verse indicates the prohibition of failing to stand firm (p-102) before the disbelievers. Allah the Exalted has explicitly stated this meaning in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you encounter those who disbelieve advancing in ranks, then do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15], up to His saying: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. And in the command to increase the remembrance of Allah the Exalted at the most constricted of times, which is the time of the clash of battle, there is clear evidence that the Muslim should increase the remembrance of Allah in every state, especially in times of distress, and the sincere lover in his love does not forget his beloved when calamities descend.

'Antarah said in his Mu'allaqah (meter: kamil):

﻿"And indeed I remembered you while the spears were drinking from me, and the Indian swords were dripping with my blood."

Another poet said:

"I remembered you while the spear (khatt) swayed between us, *** and the straight-grained, shaped spears had already quenched their thirst among us."

Note (tanbih):

Some scholars said: every "la'alla" (la'alla, "so that / perhaps") in the Qur'an is for causation (ta'lil), except the one in surah al-Shu'ara': ﴿and you take fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever﴾ [129], where it means "as if you will abide forever."

The one who restricts this (its author), may Allah pardon him, says: The word "la'alla" may occur in the speech of the Arabs intending causation, and from it is the poet's saying (meter: tawil):

"You said to us: 'Cease the wars, so that perhaps we will cease,' and you pledged to us every binding covenant. But when we ceased the war, your covenants were like a mirage shimmering in the open plain."

So his saying "la'allana nakuff" means "in order that we may cease." Its being for causation does not contradict the meaning of hope (tarajji), because the existence of the effect is hoped for when its cause exists.

The Almighty's statement: ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose heart and your strength depart﴾, and so on.

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, forbids the believers from disputing with one another, making clear that it is the cause of failure and the loss of strength. He also forbids division in other passages, such as His statement: ﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together, and do not separate﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and other similar verses. His statement in this verse, ﴿and your wind departs﴾ [al-Anfal: 46], means: your strength.

Some scholars said: "your victory," as the Arabs say, "the wind is for so-and-so," when he is dominant. From this is the poet's statement (al-Wafir meter):

"When your winds blow, seize them, for every storm has a calm."

The noun of "inna" (إنَّ) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun referring to the situation itself, placed before the clause that explains it).

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The wind" means the state of power and rule. It is likened, in the force of its command and its spread, to the wind in its blowing. So it is said: "The winds of so-and-so have blown," when fortune favours him and his command takes effect. From this is the poet's statement (al-Basit meter):

"O my two companions, is there no one in the valley
except slaves sitting among my camels?
Will you wait a little for their heedlessness,
or will you run? For the wind belongs to the aggressor."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 8, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem attractive to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed I am your protector."﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you.﴾

In this noble verse, He, exalted is He, mentions that Satan deceived the disbelievers and tricked them, and said to them: "No one can overcome you, and I am your protector."

The exegetes mention that he appeared to them in the form of "Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum" (Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum), the chief of the Banu Mudlij ibn Bakr ibn Kinanah, and said to them what Allah mentioned about him, and that he was their protector against the Banu Kinanah, and there was enmity between them. ﴿But when the two hosts sighted each other, he turned on his heels﴾ [al-Anfal: 48], when he saw the angels, and said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I see what you do not see﴾. The outcome of his affair was that he deceived them and tricked them until he brought them to destruction, then he disowned them.

This is the habit of Satan with man, as Allah, exalted is He, explained in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿Like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve," and when he disbelieves, says, "Indeed, I am free of you"﴾ [al-Hashr: 16], and His saying: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided, "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you..."﴾ [Ibrahim: 22], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, I disbelieve in what you associated me with before﴾. And like His saying: ﴿He promises them and arouses desires in them, but Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾ [an-Nisa: 120]. Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, said: [al-Basit]

We marched, and they marched to Badr in their haste; had they known the certainty of the matter, they would not have marched.
He lured them with delusion, then abandoned them; indeed, the wicked one is deceitful toward whoever follows him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 8, verse 53:

(p-104) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah never changes a blessing He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves, and indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, mentions that He does not change a blessing He has bestowed upon anyone except because of a sin that he has committed. He clarified this meaning in other verses,

• such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11],

• and His saying: ﴿And whatever disaster strikes you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30],

• and His saying: ﴿Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever bad reaches you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa: 79],

and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 8, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for those who follow you among the believers﴾.

Some scholars said: His saying ﴿and those who follow you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] is in a position of nominative case (raf') by coordination (ʿatf) with the divine name (ism al-jalalah), meaning: Allah is sufficient for you, and those among the believers who follow you are also sufficient for you.

Among those who said this is al-Hasan, and it was chosen by al-Nahhas and others, as quoted by al-Qurtubi. Other scholars said: it is in a position of genitive case (khafd) by coordination with the pronoun which is the kaf in His saying ﴿hasbaka﴾. On this view the meaning is: ﴿Allah is sufficient for you﴾, that is, sufficient for you and sufficient for those among the believers who follow you. This was said by al-Sha'bi, Ibn Zayd and others. The author of al-Kashshaf began with it, and Ibn Kathir and others confined themselves to it. The Qur'anic verses indicate the specification of the last view, namely that the meaning is: Allah is sufficient for you, and sufficient for those among the believers who follow you, because inductive survey (istiqra') of the Qur'an shows that sufficiency (hasb) and adequacy (kifayah) belong to Allah alone, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, "Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger; indeed, to Allah we are turning in hope"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 59]. He attributed the giving to Allah and His Messenger, as He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and He attributed sufficiency (hasb) to Him alone. He did not say "Allah and His Messenger are sufficient for us," but made sufficiency exclusive to Him, saying: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36]. So He restricted the adequacy which is sufficiency to Himself alone, and He praised Himself with this in His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then indeed Allah is sufficient for you. It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62]. Thus He distinguished between sufficiency (hasb) and support (ta'yid): He made sufficiency for Himself alone, and made support by His help and by His servants.

Allah, glorified and exalted, has praised the people of tawhid and tawakkul among His servants, in that they singled Him out for sufficiency (p-105). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 129], and other verses besides these.

If it is said: this view indicated by the Qur'an involves coordination with a pronoun in the genitive case without repeating the governing particle, which some scholars of Arabic grammar have declared weak. Ibn Malik said in the Khulasah, [Rajaz meter]:

"Repeating the governing particle when coordinating upon a pronoun of the genitive is made necessary."

The answer has four aspects.

The first: a group of scholars of Arabic have ruled permissible coordination without repeating the governing particle. Ibn Malik said in the Khulasah, [Rajaz meter]:

"It is not necessary in my view, since it has come, in verse and in sound prose, as established."

We have already mentioned in the surah of al-Nisa', in discussing His saying ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book﴾ [127], its grammatical evidences, and the indication of Hamzah's reading upon it, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ [al-Nisa': 1].

The second aspect: it is coordination upon the position (ʿatf ʿala al-mahall), since the kaf is genitive in position of accusative, for the meaning of ﴿hasbaka﴾ is "suffices you." Ibn Malik said in the Khulasah: [Rajaz meter]:

"The genitive of what follows what is genitive, and whoever observes the position in following, it is good."

The third aspect: it is in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿah), on the assumption of the weakness of the coordination option, as Ibn Malik said in the Khulasah: [Rajaz meter]:

"Coordination, if possible without weakness, is more deserving, and the accusative is preferred when coordination is weak."

The fourth aspect: that "man" (whoever) is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning ﴿and those who follow you among the believers﴾, then ﴿Allah is sufficient for them also﴾, so it is coordination of a sentence (ʿatf al-jumlah). And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

The author said in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

The Most High said: ﴿And those who believed but did not migrate, you have no guardianship (wilāyah) of theirs at all until they migrate.﴾

This noble verse indicates that whoever has not migrated has no guardianship (wilāyah) between him and the believers until he migrates. Yet another verse has come, from which the opposite is understood, namely the Most High's saying (p-296) ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies (awliyāʾ) of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71]. It indicates the establishment of guardianship among the believers, and its apparent meaning is generality.

The answer is in two respects:

The first: the guardianship negated in His saying ﴿you have no guardianship of theirs at all﴾ is the guardianship of inheritance (wilāyat al-mīrāth). That is, you have no share of their inheritance until they migrate, because the Muhajirun and the Ansar used to inherit from one another by the bond of brotherhood (muʾākhāh) which the Prophet ﷺ established between them. So whoever of the Muhajirun died would be inherited from by his Ansari brother, to the exclusion of his believing brother who had not migrated, until that was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying: ﴿And those related by blood are nearer to one another﴾, the verse [8].

This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, as Abu Hayyan and Ibn Jarir transmitted it from them. The guardianship in His saying ﴿the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ is the guardianship of support, aid, cooperation and mutual strengthening, because the Muslims are like a building whose parts strengthen one another, and like one body: when one of its limbs is afflicted, the rest of the body responds to it with sleeplessness and fever.

This guardianship was not intended by negation in His saying ﴿you have no guardianship of theirs at all﴾, as evidenced by His explicit statement of it in His following saying: ﴿And if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is help﴾, the verse [8]. He established the guardianship of support among them after His saying ﴿you have no guardianship of theirs at all﴾, which indicates that the guardianship negated is other than the guardianship of support. Thus it becomes clear that the guardianship negated is not the guardianship affirmed, and the difficulty is removed.

The second: this is what Ibn Kathir restricted himself to, citing as evidence a hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad and Muslim, that the meaning of His saying ﴿you have no guardianship of theirs at all﴾ is: you have no share in the spoils of war (maghānim) nor in its one-fifth (khums), except in what you have been present at in fighting. On this basis there is no difficulty in the verse, and there is no obstacle to the verse encompassing all of this, so that its meaning is the negation of inheritance between them and the negation of their being given a share of the spoils and the one-fifth.

[p. 106] The Exalted said: ﴿And those of blood relationship are nearer to one another in the Book of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, the Exalted, did not specify who is meant by *ulu al-arham* (those of blood relationship). The scholars differed over whether the Qur'an contains anything that clarifies the meaning of this verse. A group of the people of knowledge held that it was clarified by the verses of inheritance (*al-mawarith*), as we mentioned a parallel to it in His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ [An-Nisa: 7].

They said: there is no inheritance for any of those of blood relationship except those whose shares were specified in the verses of inheritance.

Among those who said this were Zayd ibn Thabit, Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, Dawud, Ibn Jarir and others. They said: what remains after the shares of the heirs whose inheritance is stipulated in the text goes to the public treasury of the Muslims (*bayt al-mal al-muslimin*). They cited the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." It was narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Amr ibn Kharija, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ.

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also narrated it from the hadith of Abu Umama, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hajar graded it as good (*hasan*). Its weakness is not established by the fact that its chain contains Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, because we have mentioned many times that his narration from the Syrians is strong. His teacher in the hadith of Abu Umama here is Shurahbil ibn Muslim, who is a Syrian and trustworthy, and he explicitly stated the transmission (*tahdith*) in his narration.

Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "truthful, with some weakness (*layyin*)." Therefore, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in this hadith, which al-Tirmidhi authenticated from the narration of Amr ibn Kharija, and which al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hajar graded as good from the narration of Abu Umama: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right," indicates by its generality that no right remains in the estate for anyone other than those whose shares were specified in the verses of inheritance.

Some of the proponents of this view said: the intended meaning of "those of blood relationship" is specifically the agnatic relatives (*al-'asaba*). They said: from this is the Arabs' saying, "a blood tie (*rahim*) has joined you," meaning the paternal kinship and not the maternal kinship. From this is also the saying of Qatilah bint al-Harith, or the daughter of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith:

[Al-Kamil]
"The swords of the sons of her father kept striking him, and by Allah, there are blood ties there that are being torn apart."

So she applied the term "blood ties" to the kinship of the sons of her father. The more apparent view, according to those who hold that there is no inheritance for them, is that the intended meaning of "those of blood relationship" is the nearer relatives whose rights were specified by the text absolutely.

Those who said "those of blood relationship do not inherit" also argued with what was narrated from Ata' ibn Yasar: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode to Quba' seeking guidance (*yastakhiru*) regarding the inheritance of the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt, and then there was revealed to him: 'There is no inheritance for them both.'" Abu Dawud recorded it in *al-Marasil* (the disconnected reports), and al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, by the route of Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata', as a *mursal* (a report in which the Companion's name is missing). Al-Nasa'i recorded it in his *Sunan*, and 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shayba, from the *mursal* of Zayd ibn Aslam, without mention of Ata'. The opponent dismissed this by saying it is a *mursal*.

It is answered that the well-known position of Malik, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad is the use of *mursal* reports as evidence. Also, al-Bayhaqi, al-Hakim and al-Tabarani narrated it connected (*mawsul*) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id. What al-Bayhaqi mentioned of its connection is through two routes:

The first: from the narration of Dirar ibn Surad Abu Nu'aym.

The second: from the narration of Shurayk ibn Abi Namir, from al-Harith ibn 'Abd, *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

The commentator on it, the author of *al-Jawhar al-Naqi*, said regarding the aforementioned Dirar that he is *matruk* (abandoned as a narrator), and attributed this to al-Nasa'i, and attributed his being declared a liar (*takdhib*) to Yahya ibn Ma'in.

He said regarding Ibn Abi Namir that there is "minor discussion" about him, and regarding al-Harith ibn 'Abd that he does not know him, and there is no mention of him except with al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* in this hadith.

The author of these notes (*muqayyiduhu*), may Allah pardon him, says: what he mentioned, that Dirar ibn Surad is *matruk*, is not correct, because he is *saduq* (truthful) with some errors that do not necessitate abandoning him.

Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "truthful, with errors and mistakes, accused of Shi'ism (*rummiya bi-al-tashayyu'*), and he was knowledgeable in the laws of inheritance (*al-fara'id*)."

As for Ibn Abi Namir, he is among the narrators of al-Bukhari and Muslim.

As for the chain of al-Hakim, al-Shawkani said of it in *Nayl al-Awtar* that it is weak. And he said regarding the chain of al-Tabarani: in it is Muhammad ibn al-Harith al-Makhzumi. I say: Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "acceptable (*maqbul*)." Al-Shawkani also said: they said that al-Tabarani also connected it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.

It is answered: he (al-Shawkani) weakened it through MaS'ada ibn al-Yasa' al-Bahili.

They said: al-Hakim also connected it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and graded it as authentic (*sahhahahu*).

It is answered: in its chain is 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far al-Madani, who is weak.

They said: al-Hakim narrated in support of it a witness report from the hadith of Shurayk ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Namir, from al-Harith ibn 'Abd, *marfu'*.

[p. 108] It is answered: in its chain is Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Shadhakuni, who is *matruk*.

They said: al-Daraqutni recorded it from another route from Shurayk.

It is answered: it is a *mursal*. End of quotation.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: these connected and disconnected routes reinforce one another, so their collection is suitable as evidence. Especially since some of them have been authenticated by some scholars, such as the route which al-Hakim authenticated. As for the weakening of it through 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far al-Madani: it is said that he is among the narrators of Muslim, and al-Bukhari cited him in suspended form (*ta'liqan*), and Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "there is nothing wrong with him." End of quotation.

They also argued with what Malik narrated in *al-Muwatta'*, and al-Bayhaqi, from Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr ibn Hazm, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Handhala al-Zuraqi: that he informed him, from a client of Quraysh who was of old called Ibn Musa, that he said: "I was sitting with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and when he had prayed the noon prayer (*al-zuhr*), he said: 'O Yarfa'! Bring that book,' meaning a book he had written concerning the matter of the paternal aunt, 'so that we may ask about it and seek information about it.' Yarfa' brought it to him, and he called for a basin or a cup containing water, and erased that book in it, then said: 'If Allah were pleased with you, He would have kept you. If Allah were pleased with you, He would have kept you.'"

Malik said in *al-Muwatta'*, from Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr ibn Hazm, that he heard his father say much: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: 'How strange is the paternal aunt, she inherits but is not inherited from.'" All of this is subject to discussion (*fihi maqal*).

A group of the people of knowledge said: there is no clarification of the verse from the Qur'an; rather, it remains upon its generality. Therefore they made inheritance obligatory for those of blood relationship.

Their definition is that they are the relatives who have no fixed share (*fard*) and no agnatic status (*ta'sib*).

They are eleven categories:

1. The children of daughters.
2. The children of sisters.
3. The daughters of brothers.
4. The children of brothers from the mother's side.
5. Paternal and maternal aunts, from all directions.
6. The maternal uncle.
7. The maternal uncles (*al-akhwal*).
8. The maternal aunts (*al-khalat*).
9. The daughters of paternal uncles.
10. The maternal grandfather (*al-jadd abu al-umm*).
11. Every grandmother who connects through a father between two mothers, or through a father higher than the grandfather.

These, and whoever connects through them, are called *dhawu al-arham* (those of blood relationship). Among those who held that they inherit when there is no heir by fixed share or agnatic status, apart from the husband and the wife, is Imam Ahmad.

This view is also narrated from 'Umar, 'Ali, 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with them all. It was also held by Shurayh, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, 'Ata', Tawus, 'Alqama, Masruq, the people of Kufa, and others.

Ibn Qudama transmitted this in *al-Mughni*. They argued with the generality of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those of blood relationship are nearer to one another﴾ [Al-Anfal: 75], and the generality of His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾, and from the Sunnah with the hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever leaves wealth, it is for his heirs, and I am the heir of whoever has no heir: I pay the blood money (*a'qilu*) on his behalf and I inherit from him. And the maternal uncle is the heir of whoever has no heir: he pays the blood money on his behalf and inherits from him." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, who both authenticated it. Abu Zur'a al-Razi graded it as good (*hasan*). Al-Bayhaqi declared it defective due to inconsistency (*idtirab*). It is reported from Yahya ibn Ma'in that he used to say: "There is no strong hadith in it." This is what al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

They also argued with what Abu Umama ibn Sahl narrated: that a man shot another man with an arrow and killed him, and he had no heir except a maternal uncle. Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah wrote about this to 'Umar, and 'Umar wrote back to him: "Indeed the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah and His Messenger are the *mawla* (protector) of whoever has no *mawla*, and the maternal uncle is the heir of whoever has no heir.'" Ahmad and Ibn Majah recorded it, and al-Tirmidhi narrated only its *marfu'* part and said: "a good hadith (*hadith hasan*)."

Al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On this subject there is also a report from 'A'isha in al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni, through the narration of Tawus, from her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The maternal uncle is the heir of whoever has no heir.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "good, strange (*hasan gharib*)." Al-Nasa'i declared it defective due to inconsistency, and al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi preferred its being a *mawquf* (a report stopping at a Companion).

Al-Tirmidhi said: Some of them have transmitted it as a *mursal* without mentioning 'A'isha.

Al-Bazzar said: "The best chain on this subject is the hadith of Abu Umama ibn Sahl." 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from a man of the people of Medina, al-'Uqayli and Ibn 'Asakir from Abu al-Darda', and Ibn al-Najjar from Abu Hurayra, all *marfu'*. End of quotation.

Al-Tirmidhi said: Most of the people of knowledge followed this hadith in holding that those of blood relationship inherit. They also argued with what Abu Dawud narrated from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, "that the Prophet ﷺ made the inheritance of the son of the one cursed (*ibn al-mula'ana*) to go to his mother and then to her heirs after her." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'a.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: In my view, the most evidentially sound of the opinions is that the maternal uncle inherits from whoever has no heir, to the exclusion of the other categories of those of blood relationship, because this is established from the Prophet ﷺ by the two hadiths mentioned, and not otherwise. For inheritance is not established except by evidence, and the generality of the two aforementioned verses does not stand as sufficient evidence, because of his saying ﷺ: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right," as has already been mentioned.

Now that you know the opinions of the scholars and their arguments regarding the inheritance of those of blood relationship and its absence, know that those who hold that they inherit differed about the manner of it. Those known among them as "the people of revelation" (*ahl al-tanzil*) held that each of them is placed in the position of the one through whom he connects to the heirs, so that his share is given to him. If they are distant, they descend degree by degree until they reach the one through whom they connect, and they take his inheritance. If there is one, he takes the whole estate; if there are several, the estate is divided among those through whom they connect. What falls to each heir is assigned to the one through whom he connects. If any of the shares of the problem (*sihham al-mas'ala*) remains, it is returned to them in proportion to their shares.

This is the position of Imam Ahmad, and it is the view of 'Alqama, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Hammad, Nu'aym, Shurayk, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri and others, as Ibn Qudama transmitted from them in *al-Mughni*.

He also said: It has been narrated from 'Ali and 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they placed a daughter's daughter in the position of a daughter, a brother's daughter in the position of a brother, a sister's daughter in the position of a sister, the paternal aunt in the position of the father, and the maternal aunt in the position of the mother. This was also narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt.

Also from 'Ali: that he placed the paternal aunt in the position of the paternal uncle. This was narrated from 'Alqama and Masruq, and it is the second narration from Ahmad. And from al-Thawri and Abu 'Ubayd: that they placed her in the position of the grandfather alongside the children of brothers and sisters, while others placed her in the position of the grandmother.

This disagreement arose regarding the paternal aunt because she connects through four inheriting lines: her father and her paternal uncle are her brothers, and her grandfather and grandmother are her parents. Those who placed the maternal aunt in the position of a grandmother did so because the grandmother is her mother. The correct view among these is to place the paternal aunt in the position of a father and the maternal aunt in the position of a mother. End of quotation from *al-Mughni*.

Another group, among those who held the doctrine of inheritance through kinship, including Abu Hanifa and his companions, went to the view that they inherit according to the order of the agnatic relatives ('asabah). They said: the children of the deceased are given precedence, however far down they go; then the children of his parents, or of one of them, however far down they go; then the children of his parents' parents, however far down they go; and so on forever. Descendants of a higher paternal ancestor do not inherit while there are descendants of a nearer paternal ancestor, even if their degree is further removed.

It is also narrated from Abu Hanifa that he placed the mother's father, however far up he goes, above the children of daughters. The school of these scholars is called the school of the people of kinship (madhhab ahl al-qarabah).

And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.
